content: The first study, identified as NCT03573570, was an interventional trial aimed at reducing anemia and other micronutrient deficiencies by providing fortified rice through the Public Distribution System (PDS) in Tamil Nadu, India. The rice was to be fortified with iron, zinc, vitamin A, and B vitamins (B1, B3, B6, B9, and B12). The trial was randomized with a parallel assignment model and no masking. The target population included children aged 6 months to 5 years, with no exclusion criteria. However, the trial was withdrawn due to the Tamil Nadu government's decision not to proceed with the implementation of fortified rice through the PDS. The principal investigator was Norman G. Miller from Stanford University. The study was first posted on June 29, 2018, and last updated on March 18, 2021. The second study, identified as NCT02532816, was an interventional trial conducted in Dompu District, Indonesia, to evaluate the effects of higher nutrient-dense complementary foods on catch-up growth and nutritional status in stunted children aged 12-23 months. The trial was randomized with quadruple masking (participant, care provider, investigator, outcomes assessor). The intervention involved complementary foods fortified with iron (75 mg as ferrous fumarate per 50 g cereal), compared to non-fortified cereal. The trial enrolled 217 participants and lasted for six months, with an additional two months of follow-up. Outcomes measured included hemoglobin levels, weight, height, mid-upper arm circumference, and usual dietary intake. The study was funded by Nestlé Company Limited (Ghana) in collaboration with the University of Ghana School of Biological Sciences. The stated purpose was to assess the impact of micronutrient-fortified complementary foods on hemoglobin, anemia prevalence, and growth in infants. The recruitment status was unknown as of August 2015. The third study, identified as Krebs 2011, was a randomized trial involving infants around six months of age. The intervention group received infant cereal fortified with zinc, while the comparator group received non-fortified cereal. The follow-up period lasted 3-4 months, and outcomes included exchangeable zinc pool size, dietary zinc intake, daily absorbed zinc, and plasma zinc levels. The study used stable isotope methods to measure zinc status in breastfed infants who were randomly assigned to one of three complementary feeding groups: infant cereal with or without zinc fortification, or meats. The study's full text was not yet available, and the publication status was limited to a conference abstract. Several other studies were excluded from analysis due to various reasons, such as wrong comparator, wrong intervention, wrong study design, or wrong population. Examples include studies that used non-fortified foods, prebiotic foods, or interventions not aligned with the research objectives. Some studies were duplicates, while others involved populations outside the target age range or used inappropriate comparators.
